Therapeutic plasma exchange in treatment of
neuroimmunologic disorders: Review of 92 cases
Mine Hayriye Sorgun a,⇑, Seyda Erdogan a, Meltem Bay b,c, Erol Ayyıldız b,c, Nezih Yücemen a,
Osman IIhan b, Canan Yücesan a

abstract
Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is a procedure that reduces amount of circulating
antibodies in patients through ﬁltration for the treatment of neurologic diseases in which
autoimmunity plays a major role. We reviewed the medical records of 92 neurologic
patients who had been consecutively treated by TPE between June 2000 and April 2011
at Ankara University School of Medicine, Neurology Department and The Apaheresis Cen-
ter. Neurological indications included myastehia gravis (MG, 16 patients), Guillain–Barre
syndrome (GBS, 37 patients) and miscellaneous diseases (39 patients). The median TPE ses-
sion number was 5 with a range of 1–8; total number of TPE procedures in all cases was
454. All MG patients improved with TPE during their hospitalization time. Regarding
GBS, nearly 67% of the patients improved early, during their hospitalization time, either.
In our series, 25% of GBS cases died because of dysautonomia. TPE was not effective in
the treatment of the patients with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic
polineuropathy, toxic polineuropathy, mononeuropathy multiplex in the case series. Dur-
ing the TPE procedures, 4 patients had hypotension and total number of the procedures
was 21 in those patients. One patient had urticaria in only one session of total 5 TPE pro-
cedures. Two patients had septicemia; the ﬁrst one had 3 and the second had 5 TPE proce-
dures; both septic cases died. In conclusion, TPE is an effective treatment in neurologic
diseases that autoimmunity plays an important role in the pathogenesis.

1. Introduction
Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is a procedure that
reduces the amount of circulating antibodies in patients
through ﬁltration for the treatment of neurologic diseases
in which autoimmunity plays a major role [1,2].I ti sa
standard treatment for some neurologic diseases such as
Guillain–Barrè syndrome (GBS) and myasthenic crisis [3–
10]. Moreover, in some other neurologic disorders, TPE
has increasingly been mentioned as a possible treatment
choice in case reports and small studies. Usually TPE is
carried out every other day for ﬁve sessions [1].
TPE is a safe procedure for the treatment of appropriate
neurologic illnesses in a specialized unit with a high
patient volume [11]. Previously we reported the response
to TPE of 50 cases with neurologic diseases [4]. Here we re-
port an additional 92 cases who were treated by TPE.
2. Methods
We reviewed the medical records of 92 neurologic pa-
tients who had been consecutively treated by TPE between
June 2000 and April 2011 at Ankara University School of

Medicine, Neurology Department and The Apaheresis
Center (TAC). Ankara has a population of approximately
4.5 million.
The medical records were analyzed for the patients
demographic details (age, sex), indications for TPE, results
of the treatment, and complications of the procedure.
Neurological indications included neuromuscular
disease (myasthenia gravis (MG), Lambert Eaton myastenic
syndrome), polyneuropathy (GBS, chronic inﬂammatory
demyelinating neuropathy (CIDP), multifocal acquired
demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy (MADSAM),
mononeuropathy multiplex, toxic polyneuropathy, parane-
oplastic polyneuropathy), demyelinization disease (multi-
ple sclerosis, transverse myelitis, acute disseminated
encephalomyelitis (ADEM), neuromyelitis optica), stiff per-
son syndrome, polymyositis, cerebellar degeneration, lim-
bic encephalitis, chorea, primary central nervous systems
vasculitis and motor neuron disease. There were 57 (62%)
female and 35 (38%) male patients. The mean age was 48
with a range of 16–77 (Std.18) ( Table 1 ). Continuous low
cell separators were used for plasma exchange in 90
patients and double cascade ﬁltration in two patients.
TPE was given every other day for most of the patients
and one plasma volume was exchanged for each session.
The mean and medianTPE session number was 5 with a
range of 1–8. Albumin was used in 15, plasma in 41, starch
in 12, and starch plus albumin in 24 patients as replace-
ment ﬂuid. All procedures in all patients were done via
vascular catheter.
The severity of abnormal ﬁndings in neurological exam-
ination at the end of TPE was compared with that before
the beginning of the treatment. If the patients’ targeted
neurologic deﬁcit improved completely (i.e. the neurologic
examination became normal), this was accepted as a ‘‘com-
plete response’’. If there was some response but the pa-
tients’ targeted neurologic deﬁcit did not disappear after
TPE (i.e. there were some abnormal ﬁndings in the neuro-
logic examination), it was accepted as a ‘‘partial response’’.
If the targeted neurologic deﬁcit did not show any
improvement after TPE (i.e. neurologic examination did
not show any change after TPE), it was classiﬁed as ‘‘no
response’’.
3. Results
The results of the treatment are summarized in Table 2.
Regarding 16 patients with MG, all of them had a myas-
thenic crisis. The patients with crisis were treated by TPE
with the aim of stabilizing the clinical picture. Thirteen pa-
tients improved completely after TPE, 2 patients responded
toTPE only partially and one patient died because of septic
shock due to catheter site infection. The TPE session num-
ber was 5 (range: 3–8) in MG cases. One patient who had
Lambert-Eaton syndrome did not respond to TPE.
TPE was started in 37 patients with GBS who were not
able to walk without assistance. They were evaluated be-
fore discharge; 4 patients improved completely (neuro-
logic examinations were normal), 20 patients improved

partially (they could walk without assistance but neuro-
logic examination was not normal). Four patients did not
show any improvement, 8 patients died because of dysau-
tonomia and one patient died because of septic shock. The
TPE session number was 4 (range: 1–6) in patients with
GBS.
Eight patients with CIDP had TPE instituted because
they needed assistance walking, and after TPE one of them
greatly improved. The response to TPE in three CIDP pa-
tients was partial, and in four CIDP patients there was no
improvement after treatment with TPE. The patient with
MADSAM was initially given steroids at 1000 mg/day for
10 days. Since there was no response to steroid therapy,
TPE was started and she showed partial improvement after
5 sessions of TPE. The patient with paraneoplastic neurop-
athy (with lung cancer) did not show any response to TPE.
Furthermore, the patient with toxic polyneuropaty and an-
other patient with mononeuropathy multiplex also did not
improve after TPE.
Nine MS cases who were in their relapse period were
treated with TPE because of the lack of response to meth-
ylprednisolone with a dosage of 1000 mg/day intrave-
nously (IV) for 10 days. Two weeks after the cessation of
IV steroid treatment, the patients were given TPE. While
2 MS patients improved totally, 6 MS patients improved
partially, and one MS patient did not show any improve-
ment after TPE. In two patients with ADEM, three with
transverse myelitis, and one with neuromyelitis optica,
methylprednisolone at a dosage of 1000 mg/day for
10 days was given at ﬁrst; however, they did not respond
to steroid therapy, then they had TPE instituted. One of
two patients with ADEM improved completely and another
one improved partially after TPE. Two patients with trans-
verse myelitis improved partially, however the last one did
not respond to TPE. The patient with neuromyelitis optica
improved partially after TPE.
Three patients with polymyositis were treated with TPE
because of the lack of response to methylprednisolone.
Two of them improved partially and the last one did not
show any improvement after TPE.
Two patients who were diagnosed with cerebellar
degeneration received out TPE because it was thought that
the cerebellar degeneration might have been secondary to
paraneoplastic diseases; one patient improved only par-
tially and the other patient did not show any improve-
ment. The response to TPE in the patient with limbic
encephalitis in whom it was thought might have had par-
aneoplastic disease was partial. Two patients with parane-
oplastic motor neuron disease were treated by TPE. One of
them improved mildly but the other one did not show any
response to TPE.
One patient had chorea with antiphospholipid antibody
and the patient improved completely after TPE. Another
patient with primary vasculitis of the central nervous sys-
tems showed mild improvement after TPE. The response to
TPE in the patient with Stiff Person syndrome was partial,
too.

(5.8%), and the total number of the procedures was 21 in
those patients. One patient had urticaria (1.2%) in only

4. Discussion
MG is a well deﬁned autoimmune disease characterized
by weakness and fatigue. Antibodies to the acetylcholine
receptor (AchR) of skeletal muscle can be detected in
80–90% of patients with generalized MG [2]. Acute
exacerbations of MG need effective and urgent life-saving
treatment. Life-threatening hypoventilation is the utmost
threat. TPE is effective for acute MG [7]. TPE can remove
AchR antibody and other immunologically active sub-
stances resulting in improvement. The efﬁcacy of TPE in
the treatment of MG varies from 55% to 100% in different
reports [3]. Plasma exchange and intravenous immuno-
globulin (IVIg) have a similar clinical effect, and a similar
responder rate. Controlled and randomized studies did
not show any difference for these two treatment options
[8,12,13]. Thirteen out of 16 MG patients improved totally
(81%, 25%) with TPE treatment in our study; two out of 16
MG cases improved partially (12%, 25%) and one patient
died because of septicemia (6%, 25%).
Lambert Eaton Syndrome is a disorder of presynaptic
neuromuscular transmission, which more frequently oc-
curs as the remote effect of a neoplasm but it may also rep-
resent without a neoplasm [14]. TPE may result in short
term improvement of Lambert Eaton Syndrome [15]. How-
ever, the patient with Lambert Eaton Syndrome did not
show any improvement after TPE in our study.
GBS presents with acute onset of progressive limb
weakness, hyporeﬂexia or areﬂexia and positive neuro-
pathic sensory symptoms [5]. Spontaneous remission oc-
curs in a larger number of cases with GBS, but the course
of the disease may be long-lasting and sometimes leads
to residual disability [2]. Treatment of GBS is centered on
TPE and IVIg [9,10]. In patients who are treated within
two weeks of onset, there is a reduction in the period of
hospitalization, in the length of time that the patients re-
quire mechanical ventilation, and in the time required to
achieve independent ambulation. TPE or intravenous
immunoglobulin infusion is instituted if the patients be-
come unable to walk unaided or if they show a signiﬁcant
reduction in vital capacity or signs of oropharyngeal weak-
ness [1,2]. Our thirty-seven patients with GBS were not
able to walk without assistance, and after treatment with
TPE, 24 patients (66.7%) had the ability to walk without
any support. Four patients did not show any improvement
(11.1%). Moreover, nine patients died (25%) because of
dysautonomia.
CIDP is an acquired, autoimmune, peripheral neurolog-
ical disorder and may cause progressive disability and even
death [2]. Treatment consist of corticosteroids, TPE, or IVIG
[16,17]. Azathioprine, rituximab, cyclophosphamide,
mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, methotrexate are
used in refractory CIDP [18]. Two randomized, controlled,
double-blinded studies provided class I evidence that TPE
is superior to placebo treatment in CIDP [16,17]. Another
study showed that the efﬁcacy of TPE in the treatment of
CIDP was 80% [19]. Only one trial has compared IVIG to
TPE in CIDP and there was no signiﬁcant difference be-
tween the two treatments [20]. In our study, eight patients
with CIDP had TPE instituted because they needed assis-

tance walking, and after treatment with TPE four of them
(50%) improved. However, the other four patients did not
respond to TPE treatment.
MADSAM neuropathy is characterized by an asymmet-
ric multifocal pattern of motor and sensory loss, and con-
duction block and other features of demyelination in
nerve conduction studies [21]. MADSAM neuropathy has
a favorable response to plasma exchange, prednisone, or
IVIG. It has been reported that 60–70% of patients with
MADSAM neuropathy showed improvement after IVIg
treatment, lasting for several months; 50–70% of patients
with MADSAM neuropathy have shown improvement with
corticosteroid treatment [22,23]. However, there is no
information about the effectiveness of TPE in MADSAM pa-
tients. Our patient with MADSAM was initially given meth-
ylprednisolone at 1000 mg/day for 10 days before TPE.
Because of a lack of response to steroids the patient had
TPE instituted. Nevertheless, she did not show any
improvement after 5 sessions of TPE.
Patients with paraneoplastic neuropathy are usually
characterized by predominant distal and sensory impair-
ment, prolonged distal motor latencies in nerve conduction
studies [24]. It has been suggested that TPE or IVIG may
provide improvement in the treatment of patients with
paraneoplastic neuropathy [24,25]. However, the response
to TPE in our patient with paraneoplastic neuropathy was
poor.
Weakness and sensory impairment of the extremities
may be caused by toxic substances such as n-hexane, hea-
vy metals, chemotheuropathic drugs [1,2,26]. We have not
found any report regarding toxic polineuropathy treatment
with TPE. Our patient with toxic polineuropathy due to n-
hexane was put on TPE treatment, however, there was no
response to TPE.

Vasculitis affecting the peripheral nerves predomi-
nantly manifests as subacute, progressive, asymmetric
sensorimotor polyneuropathy that is mononeuritis multi-
plex [1]. Therapy of mononeuritis multiplex is based on
corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide alone or in combi-
nation. Additional options include azathioprine, metho-
trexate, mycophenolate mofetil, or rituximab. In some
cases immunoglobulins or plasma exchange have been
successfully applied [1,27]. Our patient who had mononeu-
ropathy multiplex did not show any response to TPE.
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated chronic
disorder of the central nervous system (CNS) in young peo-
ple characterized by a spatial and temporal dissemination
of the pathological process [2]. When high dose intrave-
nous steroid treatment fails, TPE may provide improve-
ment with acute exacerbations of MS [28]. Our 9 MS
cases with a remitting-relapsing course were treated with
TPE because of the lack of response to methylprednisolone
with a dosage of 1000 mg/d intravenously (IV) for 10 days.
Although 6 of them (75%) did not respond to TPE, two pa-
tients (25%) improved partially.
ADEM is a central nervous system demyelinating disor-
der that is thought to be immune-mediated [1]. Clinical
improvement has been reported after initiation of cortico-
steroid therapy. There are some case reports in which TPE
was shown to be effective when treatment with corticoste-
roid fails [29]. Our 2 cases were treated with high dose
methylprednisolone for 10 days but there was no response
to steroids. Then, TPE was started. One of 2 cases with
ADEM improved completely, and the other one improved
partially after TPE.
NMO primarily affects the spinal cord and optic nerves.
In patients who did not respond to 1000 mg/d IV methyl-
prednisolone, TPE provided improvement in some studies
[28,30,31]. Our NMO patient had paraplegia and did not
show any improvement after steroid therapy, so, we tried
TPE, and the patient could walk with assistance after TPE.
Autoimmune TM is a focal disorder of the spinal cord
[1]. Treatment consists of corticosteroids, TPE, or cyclo-
phosphamide [31,32]. When high dose intravenous steroid
treatment fails, TPE may provide improvement in TM
cases. In our three patients diagnosed with transverse
myelitis they were initially given steroids at 1000 mg/day
for 10 days. However, they did not respond and they were
given 5 sessions of TPE. Finally, two patients improved par-
tially, and the other patient did not show any response to
TPE.
Chorea is rapid and jerky movements of the face, trunk,
and extremities. Chorea is sometimes associated with anti-
phospholipid antibody [33,34]. Mostly, steroids and low
dose acetylsalicylic acid have been used for treatment of
chorea associated with antiphospholipid antibodies [33].
TPE may provide improvement in some cases that do not
response to other standard therapies [35]. Our patient
had chorea with antiphospholipid antibody and the patient
improved completely after TPE.
Dermatomyositis and polymyositis are generally
responsive to prednisone, but could be refractory to them.
TPE or IVIG may provide improvement in dermatomyositis
and polymyositis cases [36–39] . Our 3 patients with poly-
myositis were treated with TPE because of the lack of re-
sponse to methylprednisolone. Two of them improved
partially and the third one did not show any response to
TPE.
It is known that paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration

may improve with TPE [40,41]. No tumor could be found
with detailed investigations including thorax and abdomen
computerized tomography and tumor markers in our two
patients with cerebeller degeneration. All other tests that
investigate the cause of cerebeller degenerations were all
normal including thyroid function tests, vasculitis markers,
vitamin E level, lipid electrophoresis. The patients were put
on TPE; one patient improved partially and the other did
not show any improvement.
To our knowledge, there is no report in the literature
regarding the effect of TPE on primary central nervous sys-
tem vasculitis cases. Our patient with vasculitis of primary
central nervous systems was treated the steroids but there
was no response. Then the patient was treated with TPE
and she improved partially.
Therapy of limbic encephalitis with or without a neo-
plasm is based on corticosteroids, IVIG, TPE and myco-
phenolat [42,43]. Our patient with limbic encephalitis did
not have a neoplasm and she was treated with TPE at ﬁrst,
however, the response to TPE was partial. Then she was
treated methylprednisolone 1000 mg/d, for 10 days, and
the patient improved completely.
Prednisone, IVIG, TPE and rituximab are used for treat-
ment of Stiff Person syndrome [38,44]. Diazepam, vigabat-
rin and baclofen provide modest relief of clinical
symptoms in Stiff Person syndrome [1,2]. Our patient with
Stiff-Person syndrome was given diazepam and baclofen,
but his symptoms did not disappear. Then he was put on
TPE and he improved partially after TPE.
There are reports showing motor neuron diseases
including paraneoplastic ones do not response to TPE
[45]. Our two patients had motor neuron disease due to
paraneoplastic syndrome. One of them improved mildly
but the other patient did not show any response to TPE.
During the TPE procedures, some complications were
reported such as hypotension, hypocalcemia, mild anemia,
urticaria, hematoma, bleeding, dysrythmia, septicemia due
to venous catheter infection requiring vasopressor support,
anaphylaxis, severe hypotension, acute pulmonary edema,
myocardial infarction, and death [4,6,46]. Our seven pa-
tients had complications such as hypotension, urticaria,
septicemia due to the venous catheter.
In summary, almost all patients with MG improved
with TPE during their hospitalization time. Regarding
GBS, nearly 67% of the patients also improved early, during
their hospitalization time. In accordance with previous lit-
erature, we suggest that TPE is an effective treatment in
cases with MG or GBS. However, in our series, even with
TPE treatment, 25% of GBS cases died because of dysauto-
nomia. One case with chorea due to antiphospholipid syn-
drome completely improved after TPE. TPE should be tried
if there is not enough response to other treatments in pa-
tients with CIDP, during relapses of RRMS, ADEM or trans-
verse myelitis. TPE may be effective in the treatment of the
patients with MADSAM, NMO, polimyositis, cerebeller
degeneration, limbic encephalitis, paraneoplastic motor
neuron disease, primary central nervous system vasculitis
178 M.H. Sorgun et al. / Transfusion and Apheresis Science 49 (2013) 174–180

and stiff person syndrome. In our case series, TPE was not
effective in the treatment of patients with Lambert-Eaton
myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic polineuropathy,
toxic polineuropathy, or mononeuropathy multiplex.
Although TPE procedures are usually safe and complica-
tions are usually manageable, our 2 cases (one with GBS,
another with MG) died because of septic shock due to ve-
nous catheter site infection. We think the complication
prevents neurology specialists from treating more patients
with TPE; instead, IVIG is preferred mostly. We suggest
that, new techniques should be developed and IV catheters
should not be needed during TPE procedures. In conclu-
sion, TPE is an effective treatment in neurologic diseases
where autoimmunity plays an important role in
pathogenesis.

logic examination was not normal). Four patients did not
show any improvement, 8 patients died because of dysau-
tonomia and one patient died because of septic shock. The
TPE session number was 4 (range: 1–6) in patients with

Eight patients with CIDP had TPE instituted because
they needed assistance walking, and after TPE one of them
greatly improved. The response to TPE in three CIDP pa-
tients was partial, and in four CIDP patients there was no
improvement after treatment with TPE. The patient with
MADSAM was initially given steroids at 1000 mg/day for
10 days. Since there was no response to steroid therapy,
TPE was started and she showed partial improvement after
5 sessions of TPE. The patient with paraneoplastic neurop-
athy (with lung cancer) did not show any response to TPE.
Furthermore, the patient with toxic polyneuropaty and an-
other patient with mononeuropathy multiplex also did not
improve after TPE.
Nine MS cases who were in their relapse period were
treated with TPE because of the lack of response to meth-
ylprednisolone with a dosage of 1000 mg/day intrave-
nously (IV) for 10 days. Two weeks after the cessation of
IV steroid treatment, the patients were given TPE. While
2 MS patients improved totally, 6 MS patients improved
partially, and one MS patient did not show any improve-
ment after TPE. In two patients with ADEM, three with
transverse myelitis, and one with neuromyelitis optica,
methylprednisolone at a dosage of 1000 mg/day for
10 days was given at ﬁrst; however, they did not respond
to steroid therapy, then they had TPE instituted. One of
two patients with ADEM improved completely and another
one improved partially after TPE. Two patients with trans-
verse myelitis improved partially, however the last one did
not respond to TPE. The patient with neuromyelitis optica
improved partially after TPE.
Three patients with polymyositis were treated with TPE
because of the lack of response to methylprednisolone.
Two of them improved partially and the last one did not
show any improvement after TPE.
Two patients who were diagnosed with cerebellar
degeneration received out TPE because it was thought that
the cerebellar degeneration might have been secondary to
paraneoplastic diseases; one patient improved only par-
tially and the other patient did not show any improve-
ment. The response to TPE in the patient with limbic
encephalitis in whom it was thought might have had par-
aneoplastic disease was partial. Two patients with parane-
oplastic motor neuron disease were treated by TPE. One of
them improved mildly but the other one did not show any
response to TPE.
One patient had chorea with antiphospholipid antibody
and the patient improved completely after TPE. Another
patient with primary vasculitis of the central nervous sys-
tems showed mild improvement after TPE. The response to
TPE in the patient with Stiff Person syndrome was partial,
too.

4. Discussion
MG is a well deﬁned autoimmune disease characterized
by weakness and fatigue. Antibodies to the acetylcholine
receptor (AchR) of skeletal muscle can be detected in
80–90% of patients with generalized MG [2]. Acute
exacerbations of MG need effective and urgent life-saving
treatment. Life-threatening hypoventilation is the utmost
threat. TPE is effective for acute MG [7]. TPE can remove
AchR antibody and other immunologically active sub-
stances resulting in improvement. The efﬁcacy of TPE in
the treatment of MG varies from 55% to 100% in different
reports [3]. Plasma exchange and intravenous immuno-
globulin (IVIg) have a similar clinical effect, and a similar
responder rate. Controlled and randomized studies did
not show any difference for these two treatment options
[8,12,13]. Thirteen out of 16 MG patients improved totally
(81%, 25%) with TPE treatment in our study; two out of 16
MG cases improved partially (12%, 25%) and one patient
died because of septicemia (6%, 25%).
Lambert Eaton Syndrome is a disorder of presynaptic
neuromuscular transmission, which more frequently oc-
curs as the remote effect of a neoplasm but it may also rep-
resent without a neoplasm [14]. TPE may result in short
term improvement of Lambert Eaton Syndrome [15]. How-
ever, the patient with Lambert Eaton Syndrome did not
show any improvement after TPE in our study.
GBS presents with acute onset of progressive limb
weakness, hyporeﬂexia or areﬂexia and positive neuro-
pathic sensory symptoms [5]. Spontaneous remission oc-
curs in a larger number of cases with GBS, but the course
of the disease may be long-lasting and sometimes leads
to residual disability [2]. Treatment of GBS is centered on
TPE and IVIg [9,10]. In patients who are treated within
two weeks of onset, there is a reduction in the period of
hospitalization, in the length of time that the patients re-
quire mechanical ventilation, and in the time required to
achieve independent ambulation. TPE or intravenous
immunoglobulin infusion is instituted if the patients be-
come unable to walk unaided or if they show a signiﬁcant
reduction in vital capacity or signs of oropharyngeal weak-
ness [1,2]. Our thirty-seven patients with GBS were not
able to walk without assistance, and after treatment with
TPE, 24 patients (66.7%) had the ability to walk without
any support. Four patients did not show any improvement
(11.1%). Moreover, nine patients died (25%) because of
dysautonomia.
CIDP is an acquired, autoimmune, peripheral neurolog-
ical disorder and may cause progressive disability and even
death [2]. Treatment consist of corticosteroids, TPE, or IVIG
[16,17]. Azathioprine, rituximab, cyclophosphamide,
mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, methotrexate are
used in refractory CIDP [18]. Two randomized, controlled,
double-blinded studies provided class I evidence that TPE
is superior to placebo treatment in CIDP [16,17]. Another
study showed that the efﬁcacy of TPE in the treatment of
CIDP was 80% [19]. Only one trial has compared IVIG to
TPE in CIDP and there was no signiﬁcant difference be-
tween the two treatments [20]. In our study, eight patients
with CIDP had TPE instituted because they needed assis-

segments.text:
tance walking, and after treatment with TPE four of them
(50%) improved. However, the other four patients did not
respond to TPE treatment.
MADSAM neuropathy is characterized by an asymmet-
ric multifocal pattern of motor and sensory loss, and con-
duction block and other features of demyelination in
nerve conduction studies [21]. MADSAM neuropathy has
a favorable response to plasma exchange, prednisone, or
IVIG. It has been reported that 60–70% of patients with
MADSAM neuropathy showed improvement after IVIg
treatment, lasting for several months; 50–70% of patients
with MADSAM neuropathy have shown improvement with
corticosteroid treatment [22,23]. However, there is no
information about the effectiveness of TPE in MADSAM pa-
tients. Our patient with MADSAM was initially given meth-
ylprednisolone at 1000 mg/day for 10 days before TPE.
Because of a lack of response to steroids the patient had
TPE instituted. Nevertheless, she did not show any
improvement after 5 sessions of TPE.
Patients with paraneoplastic neuropathy are usually
characterized by predominant distal and sensory impair-
ment, prolonged distal motor latencies in nerve conduction
studies [24]. It has been suggested that TPE or IVIG may
provide improvement in the treatment of patients with
paraneoplastic neuropathy [24,25]. However, the response
to TPE in our patient with paraneoplastic neuropathy was
poor.
Weakness and sensory impairment of the extremities
may be caused by toxic substances such as n-hexane, hea-
vy metals, chemotheuropathic drugs [1,2,26]. We have not
found any report regarding toxic polineuropathy treatment
with TPE. Our patient with toxic polineuropathy due to n-
hexane was put on TPE treatment, however, there was no
response to TPE.

Vasculitis affecting the peripheral nerves predomi-
nantly manifests as subacute, progressive, asymmetric
sensorimotor polyneuropathy that is mononeuritis multi-
plex [1]. Therapy of mononeuritis multiplex is based on
corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide alone or in combi-
nation. Additional options include azathioprine, metho-
trexate, mycophenolate mofetil, or rituximab. In some
cases immunoglobulins or plasma exchange have been
successfully applied [1,27]. Our patient who had mononeu-
ropathy multiplex did not show any response to TPE.
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated chronic
disorder of the central nervous system (CNS) in young peo-
ple characterized by a spatial and temporal dissemination
of the pathological process [2]. When high dose intrave-
nous steroid treatment fails, TPE may provide improve-
ment with acute exacerbations of MS [28]. Our 9 MS
cases with a remitting-relapsing course were treated with
TPE because of the lack of response to methylprednisolone
with a dosage of 1000 mg/d intravenously (IV) for 10 days.
Although 6 of them (75%) did not respond to TPE, two pa-
tients (25%) improved partially.
ADEM is a central nervous system demyelinating disor-
der that is thought to be immune-mediated [1]. Clinical
improvement has been reported after initiation of cortico-
steroid therapy. There are some case reports in which TPE
was shown to be effective when treatment with corticoste-
roid fails [29]. Our 2 cases were treated with high dose
methylprednisolone for 10 days but there was no response
to steroids. Then, TPE was started. One of 2 cases with
ADEM improved completely, and the other one improved
partially after TPE.
NMO primarily affects the spinal cord and optic nerves.
In patients who did not respond to 1000 mg/d IV methyl-
prednisolone, TPE provided improvement in some studies
[28,30,31]. Our NMO patient had paraplegia and did not
show any improvement after steroid therapy, so, we tried
TPE, and the patient could walk with assistance after TPE.
Autoimmune TM is a focal disorder of the spinal cord
[1]. Treatment consists of corticosteroids, TPE, or cyclo-
phosphamide [31,32]. When high dose intravenous steroid
treatment fails, TPE may provide improvement in TM
cases. In our three patients diagnosed with transverse
myelitis they were initially given steroids at 1000 mg/day
for 10 days. However, they did not respond and they were
given 5 sessions of TPE. Finally, two patients improved par-
tially, and the other patient did not show any response to
TPE.
Chorea is rapid and jerky movements of the face, trunk,
and extremities. Chorea is sometimes associated with anti-
phospholipid antibody [33,34]. Mostly, steroids and low
dose acetylsalicylic acid have been used for treatment of
chorea associated with antiphospholipid antibodies [33].
TPE may provide improvement in some cases that do not
response to other standard therapies [35]. Our patient
had chorea with antiphospholipid antibody and the patient
improved completely after TPE.
Dermatomyositis and polymyositis are generally
responsive to prednisone, but could be refractory to them.
TPE or IVIG may provide improvement in dermatomyositis
and polymyositis cases [36–39] . Our 3 patients with poly-
myositis were treated with TPE because of the lack of re-
sponse to methylprednisolone. Two of them improved
partially and the third one did not show any response to
TPE.
It is known that paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration

segments.text:
may improve with TPE [40,41]. No tumor could be found
with detailed investigations including thorax and abdomen
computerized tomography and tumor markers in our two
patients with cerebeller degeneration. All other tests that
investigate the cause of cerebeller degenerations were all
normal including thyroid function tests, vasculitis markers,
vitamin E level, lipid electrophoresis. The patients were put
on TPE; one patient improved partially and the other did
not show any improvement.
To our knowledge, there is no report in the literature
regarding the effect of TPE on primary central nervous sys-
tem vasculitis cases. Our patient with vasculitis of primary
central nervous systems was treated the steroids but there
was no response. Then the patient was treated with TPE
and she improved partially.
Therapy of limbic encephalitis with or without a neo-
plasm is based on corticosteroids, IVIG, TPE and myco-
phenolat [42,43]. Our patient with limbic encephalitis did
not have a neoplasm and she was treated with TPE at ﬁrst,
however, the response to TPE was partial. Then she was
treated methylprednisolone 1000 mg/d, for 10 days, and
the patient improved completely.
Prednisone, IVIG, TPE and rituximab are used for treat-
ment of Stiff Person syndrome [38,44]. Diazepam, vigabat-
rin and baclofen provide modest relief of clinical
symptoms in Stiff Person syndrome [1,2]. Our patient with
Stiff-Person syndrome was given diazepam and baclofen,
but his symptoms did not disappear. Then he was put on
TPE and he improved partially after TPE.
There are reports showing motor neuron diseases
including paraneoplastic ones do not response to TPE
[45]. Our two patients had motor neuron disease due to
paraneoplastic syndrome. One of them improved mildly
but the other patient did not show any response to TPE.
During the TPE procedures, some complications were
reported such as hypotension, hypocalcemia, mild anemia,
urticaria, hematoma, bleeding, dysrythmia, septicemia due
to venous catheter infection requiring vasopressor support,
anaphylaxis, severe hypotension, acute pulmonary edema,
myocardial infarction, and death [4,6,46]. Our seven pa-
tients had complications such as hypotension, urticaria,
septicemia due to the venous catheter.
In summary, almost all patients with MG improved
with TPE during their hospitalization time. Regarding
GBS, nearly 67% of the patients also improved early, during
their hospitalization time. In accordance with previous lit-
erature, we suggest that TPE is an effective treatment in
cases with MG or GBS. However, in our series, even with
TPE treatment, 25% of GBS cases died because of dysauto-
nomia. One case with chorea due to antiphospholipid syn-
drome completely improved after TPE. TPE should be tried
if there is not enough response to other treatments in pa-
tients with CIDP, during relapses of RRMS, ADEM or trans-
verse myelitis. TPE may be effective in the treatment of the
patients with MADSAM, NMO, polimyositis, cerebeller
degeneration, limbic encephalitis, paraneoplastic motor
neuron disease, primary central nervous system vasculitis
178 M.H. Sorgun et al. / Transfusion and Apheresis Science 49 (2013) 174–180

segments.text:
and stiff person syndrome. In our case series, TPE was not
effective in the treatment of patients with Lambert-Eaton
myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic polineuropathy,
toxic polineuropathy, or mononeuropathy multiplex.
Although TPE procedures are usually safe and complica-
tions are usually manageable, our 2 cases (one with GBS,
another with MG) died because of septic shock due to ve-
nous catheter site infection. We think the complication
prevents neurology specialists from treating more patients
with TPE; instead, IVIG is preferred mostly. We suggest
that, new techniques should be developed and IV catheters
should not be needed during TPE procedures. In conclu-
sion, TPE is an effective treatment in neurologic diseases
where autoimmunity plays an important role in
pathogenesis.
